questions.q: In API testing, what is an endpoint?
choices: The server that hosts the API's documentation
A location where the API receives requests about a specific resource
The last response in a sequence of API calls
A rate limit applied to each API client
questions.explain: In GET /api/books, for example, the endpoint is /api/books, which returns a list of books. /api/books/mystery would be a different endpoint that returns mystery books.

questions.q: During API recon, what do you need to work out about an endpoint so you can build valid requests to it?
choices: Which parameters are compulsory and which are optional
Which HTTP methods and media formats it accepts
Its rate limits and authentication mechanisms
Which programming language its developers prefer
questions.explain: Recon is about the attack surface: the input data the API takes (compulsory and optional), the request types it accepts (methods and media formats), and its rate limits and authentication mechanisms.

questions.q: Machine-readable API documentation is meant to be processed by software. Which formats does it typically use?
questions.explain: Machine-readable docs use structured formats such as JSON or XML so tools can automate integration and validation. Human-readable docs are written for developers and contain explanations, examples, and usage scenarios.

questions.q: You spot a request to /api/swagger/v1/users/123. What is a good way to look for the API's documentation?
questions.explain: Investigating base paths can lead you to documentation. You can also run Intruder with a list of common documentation paths.

questions.q: Which of these paths could point to API documentation?
questions.explain: /api, /swagger/index.html, and /openapi.json are common documentation locations. /favicon.ico is just the site icon.

questions.q: If you already have the API documentation, you can skip browsing the application to identify endpoints.
questions.explain: Documentation can be inaccurate or out of date. Browse the app anyway: crawl it with Burp Scanner, then explore manually in Burp's browser.

questions.q: Why review an application's JavaScript files during endpoint discovery?
choices: They contain the server's database credentials
They can reference API endpoints you haven't triggered from the browser
They define the API's rate limits
They run on the server, so they reveal server-side logic
questions.explain: JavaScript can reference endpoints your browsing never triggered. Burp Scanner extracts some of them during crawls. For heavier extraction, use the JS Link Finder BApp or read the JS manually in Burp.

questions.q: Classic vulnerabilities such as SQL injection can count as part of API testing.
questions.explain: Every dynamic website is built from APIs, so classic web vulnerabilities like SQLi can also be seen as API testing.

questions.q: Which HTTP method asks the server which methods are allowed on a resource?
questions.explain: OPTIONS lists the methods allowed on a resource. GET retrieves data and PATCH applies partial changes.

questions.q: Which HTTP method applies partial changes to a resource?
questions.explain: PATCH applies partial changes. GET retrieves data and OPTIONS lists the allowed methods.

questions.q: Once you know which HTTP method the front-end uses for an endpoint, there's no point testing other methods on it.
questions.explain: One endpoint can support several methods. For example, GET /api/tasks lists tasks, POST /api/tasks creates one, and DELETE /api/tasks/1 deletes one. Test them all to find more functionality. Burp Intruder's built-in "HTTP verbs" list can cycle through them.

questions.q: When cycling through HTTP methods on an endpoint, why should you target low-priority objects?
choices: High-priority objects never accept non-GET methods
Low-priority objects aren't logged by the server
So you don't alter critical items or create too many records
questions.explain: Methods like DELETE, PUT, or POST can change or create data. Testing on low-priority objects avoids unintended consequences.

questions.q: What can changing the content type of an API request achieve?
choices: Trigger errors that disclose useful information
Exploit differences in processing logic, e.g. an API that is safe with JSON but injectable with XML
questions.explain: A different content type can expose errors, slip past flawed defenses, or reach different processing logic. Nothing guarantees that authentication gets skipped.

questions.q: How do you change the content type of an API request when testing?
choices: Change only the body and leave the headers alone
Add a .xml extension to the URL
Change the Content-Type header and reformat the request body to match
Change the HTTP method to OPTIONS
questions.explain: Change the Content-Type header and reformat the body to match. The Content type converter BApp converts request data between XML and JSON.

questions.q: You've found PUT /api/user/update. How could Burp Intruder help you find hidden endpoints?
choices: Put a payload position at /update and try words like delete and add
Fuzz the Host header with IP addresses
Replay the request with every HTTP status code
questions.explain: Swap the /update segment for candidate names. Build the wordlist from common API naming conventions, industry terms, and app-specific terms you found during recon.

questions.q: API error messages are worth reading closely, since they can show you how to build a valid request.
questions.explain: Error messages often reveal what the API expects, such as parameters, formats, or types. That helps you build valid requests.

questions.q: What is mass assignment?
choices: Sending the same request to many endpoints at once
A framework automatically binding request parameters to fields on an internal object, so the app accepts parameters the developer never meant it to process
Assigning many users to the same role through the admin panel
Overriding a query parameter by supplying it twice
questions.explain: Mass assignment (auto-binding) creates hidden parameters by accident. Supplying a parameter twice describes the parameter override in server-side parameter pollution.

questions.q: Mass assignment is also known by what other name?
questions.explain: It's also called auto-binding because the framework binds request parameters to object fields automatically.

questions.q: PATCH /api/users/ sends username and email. GET /api/users/123 returns id, name, email, and isAdmin. Which fields are likely hidden parameters bound to the user object?
questions.explain: id and isAdmin appear in the returned object but not in the update request, so they are probably bound to the same internal user object. email and username are already sent by the PATCH request.

questions.q: To test a suspected isAdmin parameter, you send "isAdmin": false and then "isAdmin": "foo". The app behaves differently for "foo". What does that suggest?
choices: The app is vulnerable to SQL injection
The invalid value affects query logic, so the parameter may be user-updatable
questions.explain: A different response to the invalid value means the parameter is being processed. The next step is to send "isAdmin": true and check whether the account now has admin functionality.

questions.q: Mass assignment works because the bound parameter's value is accepted without adequate validation or sanitization.
questions.explain: The framework binds the value straight onto the object. Without validation, a user can set fields like isAdmin.

questions.q: How does Burp Intruder help find hidden parameters?
choices: It uses a wordlist of common parameter names to replace existing parameters or add new ones
It decompiles the server's source code
It reads the server's environment variables
It only tests parameters listed in the documentation
questions.explain: Intruder fuzzes with common parameter names, and you should add app-relevant ones. The Param miner BApp automates this, guessing up to 65,536 parameter names per request.

questions.q: Which practices help prevent API vulnerabilities?
choices: Validate the expected content type for each request and response
Protect only the current production version of the API
questions.explain: Protect every API version, not just the current production one. Older versions are still part of the attack surface.

questions.q: Which defense addresses mass assignment?
choices: Use verbose error messages so developers can debug faster
Allowlist the properties users may update and blocklist sensitive properties
Accept any content type the client sends
questions.explain: Explicitly control which properties can be bound: allowlist the updatable ones and blocklist sensitive ones like isAdmin.

questions.q: Keeping API documentation up to date helps security, because legitimate testers can then see the full attack surface.
questions.explain: Outdated docs hide endpoints and parameters from legitimate testers, so those parts never get tested.

questions.q: An API isn't meant for public use. What should happen to its documentation?
choices: Publish it anyway so nothing looks hidden
Secure it so it isn't publicly accessible
Remove the error message section from it
questions.explain: Public docs hand attackers a map of the attack surface. Secure them if the API isn't intended to be public.

questions.q: What is the main defense against server-side parameter pollution?
choices: Use a WAF that strips duplicate parameters
Switch the internal API from JSON to XML
Allowlist characters that don't need encoding and encode all other user input before it goes into a server-side request
questions.explain: Encode user input before embedding it in server-side requests, apart from an allowlist of safe characters. Also check that input matches the expected format and structure.

questions.q: Checking that user input matches the expected format and structure helps prevent server-side parameter pollution.
questions.explain: Format and structure validation, together with encoding, stops injected syntax from reaching the internal API.

questions.q: What is server-side parameter pollution (SSPP)?
choices: A website embeds user input in a server-side request to an internal API without adequate encoding
Polluting a JavaScript object's prototype on the server
Flooding an API with requests to exhaust its resources
Hiding parameters in the URL fragment so the server never sees them
questions.explain: SSPP lets an attacker override existing parameters, change app behavior, or access unauthorized data. It targets internal APIs that can't be reached from the internet, and it has almost nothing to do with server-side prototype pollution.

questions.q: Which kinds of user input could be vulnerable to SSPP?
questions.explain: Any user input that ends up embedded in a server-side request to an internal API can be vulnerable.

questions.q: Why must you send # as %23 when trying to truncate a server-side query string?
choices: The internal API only reads hexadecimal
Unencoded, # is treated as a fragment identifier and is never passed on to the internal API
An unencoded # always triggers the WAF
questions.explain: Encoding it as %23 gets the # to the back end, where it is decoded and can cut off the rest of the internal query string.

questions.q: The browser sends GET /userSearch?name=peter%23foo&back=/home, and the server calls GET /users/search?name=peter#foo&publicProfile=true. The response returns the user peter. What does this suggest?
choices: foo was treated as part of the username
The server-side query may have been truncated at the #
The parameter was injected but ignored
questions.explain: Getting peter back means everything after # was probably dropped. An "Invalid name" response would instead mean foo was treated as part of the username, so the query probably wasn't truncated.

questions.q: In that example, what is the potential impact of truncating the internal query?
choices: The publicProfile=true condition is dropped, which may expose non-public profiles
The request switches from GET to POST
The response's content type changes to XML
questions.explain: Truncation removes the server-added publicProfile=true restriction, so the internal API may return profiles that aren't public.

questions.q: When injecting an extra parameter into a server-side query string, what URL-encoded sequence do you send for the & character?
questions.explain: For example, name=peter%26foo=xyz becomes name=peter&foo=xyz&publicProfile=true in the internal request.

questions.q: You send name=peter%26foo=xyz and the response is unchanged. What can you conclude?
choices: The site is definitely not vulnerable
The parameter may have been injected but ignored, so you need more tests
questions.explain: An unchanged response is ambiguous. Next, try injecting a valid parameter (e.g. %26email=foo) or overriding an existing one.

questions.q: What does the payload name=peter%26name=carlos attempt?
choices: To override the existing name parameter with a second one of the same name
To truncate the internal query string
To traverse to a parent directory in a REST path
To change the request's content type
questions.explain: It produces name=peter&name=carlos&publicProfile=true internally. How the back end handles the duplicate depends on its technology, and a changed response confirms SSPP.

questions.q: The internal API runs on PHP and receives name=peter&name=carlos. What happens?
choices: It searches for peter, because only the first parameter is used
It searches for carlos, because only the last parameter is used
It rejects the request for having duplicate parameters
questions.explain: PHP uses the last parameter only, so the search is for carlos.

questions.q: The internal API runs on ASP.NET and receives name=peter&name=carlos. What happens?
choices: It combines both values into peter,carlos, which may give an Invalid username error
questions.explain: ASP.NET combines duplicate parameters, so the search is for peter,carlos, which may not be a valid username.

questions.q: The internal API runs on Node.js/Express and receives name=peter&name=carlos. What happens?
choices: It combines both values into peter,carlos
It returns an error for duplicate parameters
It uses only the first parameter, so the result for peter is unchanged
questions.explain: Node.js/Express uses the first parameter, so the response doesn't change, even though the injection did happen.

questions.q: You've confirmed you can override the name parameter in an internal request. Which injection could let you act as a privileged user?
questions.explain: Overriding name with administrator may let you log in as the administrator account.

questions.category: SSPP in REST paths & structured data
questions.q: In the REST URL /api/users/123, what does /123 represent?
questions.explain: /api is the root API endpoint, /users is the resource, and /123 is a parameter. RESTful APIs often put parameters in the URL path instead of the query string.

questions.category: SSPP in REST paths & structured data
questions.q: GET /edit_profile.php?name=peter makes the server request GET /api/private/users/peter. Which payload tests for SSPP in the REST path?
questions.explain: Encoded path traversal sequences (%2f = /) produce /api/private/users/peter/../admin in the internal request.

questions.category: SSPP in REST paths & structured data
questions.q: The server-side client or back-end API normalizes /api/private/users/peter/../admin. Which path does it end up requesting?
questions.explain: The ../ cancels the peter segment, which leaves /api/private/users/admin.

questions.category: SSPP in REST paths & structured data
questions.q: POST /myaccount with name=peter makes the server send PATCH /users/7312/update with {"name":"peter"}. Which form value could make peter an administrator if the input isn't validated or encoded?
questions.explain: The quotes close the name string and add a new key, so the server builds {"name":"peter","access_level":"administrator"}.

questions.category: SSPP in REST paths & structured data
questions.q: Structured-data SSPP can only happen in requests, never in responses.
questions.explain: Input stored safely in a database can later be embedded in a back-end API's JSON response without encoding. You detect and exploit that the same way as in requests.

questions.category: SSPP in REST paths & structured data
questions.q: Structured-data injection can happen in any structured format. Which attack is an XML example?
questions.explain: XInclude attacks inject XML structure into server-side XML documents (covered under XXE).

questions.category: SSPP in REST paths & structured data
questions.q: When Burp Scanner flags a suspicious input transformation, that alone confirms a vulnerability.
questions.explain: A transformation (input received, transformed, then processed) is only a lead and needs manual confirmation. Likewise, inputs that Backslash Powered Scanner classifies as "interesting" should be investigated manually.

questions.q: OWASP's "Broken object property level authorization" risk corresponds to which vulnerability?
questions.explain: Letting users set object properties they shouldn't be able to set, such as isAdmin, is mass assignment.

questions.q: Which OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) risks map to access control / privilege escalation?
questions.explain: Both object-level and function-level authorization risks are access control problems. Broken authentication maps to authentication, OAuth 2.0, and JWT attacks.

questions.q: OWASP's "Unrestricted access to sensitive business flows" risk corresponds to which vulnerability class?
questions.explain: Abusing sensitive business flows is a business logic flaw.

questions.q: OWASP's "Unrestricted resource consumption" risk relates to which vulnerability classes?
questions.explain: Race conditions and file upload vulnerabilities both involve resource consumption that the API doesn't adequately limit.

questions.q: OWASP's "Security misconfiguration" risk relates to which vulnerability classes?
questions.explain: Security misconfiguration covers CORS, information disclosure, HTTP Host header attacks, and HTTP request smuggling. Mass assignment is broken object property level authorization.

questions.q: Which OWASP API Security Top 10 risks map directly to API testing itself?
questions.explain: Improper inventory management (e.g. undocumented or old API versions) and unsafe consumption of APIs are covered by API testing. Broken authentication and SSRF have their own topics.
